# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Paper 1 replicated the conditional-logit win model of @owen2019 — one of
a line of discrete-choice race models reaching back to @boltonchapman1986
— on UK All-Weather (AW) Flat handicaps and found that the model trails
the betting market across the full threshold range, returning
`r scales::percent(backtest_naive$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` on the §3.4
backtest. We diagnosed the shortfall as a problem of *discrimination*
rather than calibration: a thirteen-feature predictor set is too thin to
compete with a starting price that already aggregates weight, draw,
going, jockey, recent form and informed money. This paper keeps the win
objective and the data fixed, and asks how far a richer feature set can
narrow that gap.

We make two contributions. First, an **extended feature set**, evaluated
with an automated univariate screen — a standalone conditional logit per
candidate, ranked by a McFadden pseudo-$R^2$ against the
equal-probability null, following @juola2018. Second, **race-level
interactions** through the mixed discrete-choice formulation: distance
and course are constant within a race and so cancel in the softmax, but
their products with horse-level features vary across runners and can
enter the model — and this recovers a course-specific draw bias invisible
to a win model with a single pooled draw term. Data scope, race selection
and the train/test split are unchanged from paper 1.

The win-model ROI moves from
`r scales::percent(backtest_naive$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` in paper 1 to
`r scales::percent(backtest_naive_w_final$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` in the
final model — a narrowing that is directionally consistent but, on a
paired race-level bootstrap of the ROI difference, not statistically
distinguishable from zero; the market still dominates. The official rating
(`or_relative`) is the strongest new predictor, and the draw × course
interaction produces the single largest backtest improvement. The
market-efficiency interpretation of paper 1 is sustained, perhaps slightly
weakened. The companion paper 2b keeps this feature set fixed and changes
the objective — from predicting the win to predicting the finishing order
— to ask whether the ranking likelihood extracts more from the same
features.

The paper is organised as follows. @sec-data sets out the data, the
two-tier feature set and the three data decisions specific to this paper.
@sec-eda evaluates every candidate feature through the univariate screen
and records the feature drop and keep decisions. @sec-extended-win fits
the extended win model and contrasts it with paper 1 and Owen's Table 3.
@sec-mixed-interactions tests the two race-level interactions and selects
the final model. @sec-discussion draws the threads together and signposts
papers 2b and 3, and @sec-appx-derivations derives the mixed-choice
machinery in full.

# Acknowledgments {.unnumbered}

I have been interested in modelling horse racing since first
acquiring the Smartform database more than a decade ago. The project
has been picked up and put down many times, the obstacle almost
always being the gap between an idea and a running implementation.
What is different now is that working alongside Claude Code
(Anthropic's coding agent), with web-based Claude as a research
companion, has compressed that gap dramatically. I am grateful to
my brother, Michael Gillen, for the suggestion to build the model
on All-Weather races — the foundation of the scope choices set out
in @sec-data. The design choices — dataset, scope, model,
comparison, editorial line — are mine. The implementation, the bulk
of the draft prose, and a great deal of the verification were
Claude Code's, under my direction; every output was reviewed and
edited before it reached the paper. I do not yet know what general
lessons this experiment points to about the value of human–AI
collaboration in applied statistics. That uncertainty is part of
why I am doing the work, and these papers are partly a record of
that experiment.
